paras.text: The current study was approved by the University of New Brunswick’s institutional review board (REB # 2024-012). All aspects of this study, including the recruitment plan, procedure, and analyses, received in principle (Stage I) acceptance through Peer Community in Registered Reports (https://osf.io/3u7eh). Using G*Power (Faul et al., 2009), and specifying “Repeated measures, within factors” per our planned analysis specified below, it was determined that 82 total participants would be required to achieve power of 0.95 to detect a medium effect size (d = 0.37), which would be consistent with past work on the phenomenon (see Bertsch et al., 2007, for a review). The effect size included in the power analysis reflects the main effect of task type (read versus generate) we expected to observe. We also tested an interaction effect between task type and sensory modality, which we expected would yield at least a medium effect size, given that both overt and covert generation tasks yield similar effect sizes (see McCurdy et al., 2020, for a review).

The stimuli used for the current study were 120 word pairs taken from the Nelson free association norms (Nelson et al., 2004; see supplementary materials). All materials have been uploaded to an online repository (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/SKQR7). The cue and target words of each word pair are semantically associated (forward associative strength: M = 0.23, SD = 0.08, range = 0.102–0.397; backward associative strength: 0; letter length: M = 6.49, SD = 0.16, range = 3–11). Using a fully within-subjects counterbalanced blocked design, some participants were first exposed to the completed word pair lists under the reading conditions, and the other participants first received the incomplete word pair lists—which contained only the cue words and the first letter of each target word—for the generation tasks. The experiment was programmed and administered using PsychoPy, a freely available software for conducting psychological studies (Peirce et al., 2019). All stimuli were presented using this software, in addition to instructions about whether the stimuli would be presented through an auditory, visual, or multisensory modality preceding each condition. Instructions and practice trials were presented at the beginning of the study.

The generation effect refers to the advantage in memory performance for verbal information when it is generated by one’s own mind, rather than passively read (Slamecka & Graf, 1978). The effect is robust, improving both item memory (word-specific) and context memory (information surrounding the word; McCurdy et al., 2020). Although the generation task often inherently involves a multisensory process of interpreting visual stimuli, and vocalizing the text to produce its auditory representation, this aspect of the task has not been explicitly investigated. One specific aim of the current study was to examine whether the generation effect is moderated by multisensory processing.

The ability to efficiently process multisensory information is a capacity finely tuned to accommodate humans’ multisensory way of living (Shams & Seitz, 2008). Complex neural networks throughout the brain support the simultaneous integration and processing of multisensory information (Burton et al., 2002; Falchier et al., 2002; Ghazanfar & Schroeder, 2006; Rockland & Ojima, 2003; Röder et al., 2002). Humans respond and adapt to the multiple sources of information in the environment and reduce cognitive load by pairing congruent stimuli together. Consequently, fewer cognitive resources are needed to process congruent stimuli (Fahey et al., 2018; Shams & Seitz, 2008). Shams and Seitz (2008) define congruent stimuli as “[…] the relationship between stimuli that are consistent with the prior experience of the individual or relationships between the senses found in nature” (p.2). By this definition, arbitrary associations between auditory and visual stimuli will not bring about a multisensory facilitation effect. Interestingly, if two stimuli are paired for the purpose of a specific task that are not semantically co-occurring in nature (e.g., an auditory input of a dog barking paired with an image of a lion), integration of these two stimuli during encoding is still possible (Moran et al., 2013). In long-term memory, however, only partial or occasional integration at the subconscious level will occur, leading to deleterious effects of multisensory input of stimuli in such a scenario (Moran et al., 2013; Shams et al., 2011). Congruent pairings are developed within an individual’s semantic network through repeated exposure to those pairings. When associated visual and auditory stimuli are presented together, processing of either stimulus will be facilitated because of a more elaborate representation of the information across the semantic network (Moran et al., 2013; Shams et al., 2011).

Importantly, successful multisensory processing of a single experience is contingent on temporal binding, whereby information acquired from each sense be provided within a certain window of time so that the percepts may be unified as a coherent perception (Meredith et al., 1992; Wallace et al., 1996; Wallace & Stevenson, 2014). Failure to adhere to the window could result in the perception of two unintegrated unisensory experiences in lieu of one multisensory percept (Wallace et al., 2004; Stevenson et al., 2012). The precise timing during which stimuli from various modalities are prone to perceptual binding is debated as being as little as 50–100 ms (Slutsky & Recanzone, 2001) to as great as 800 ms (Wallace et al., 2004). Ultimately, the simultaneous presentation of multiple stimuli ensures that auditory and visual stimuli are perceived concordantly, as the temporal window between stimuli provides statistical cues to their relationship (Wallace & Stevenson, 2014).

A notable benefit of multisensory processing is its apparent facilitation effect, wherein unisensory items exhibit enhanced recognition when paired with congruent sensory inputs. Seitz et al. (2006) demonstrated that participants recognized visual stimuli that were paired with concurrent auditory stimuli after approximately 60% fewer training sessions than those who studied visual stimuli in isolation. Multisensory integration may reduce the overall uncertainty in the sensory estimates, leading to more reliable and precise responses (Alais & Burr, 2004). Connections are established through the multisensory learning conditions (Seitz et al., 2006) and any aspect of the multisensory representation can be elicited by merely activating a unisensory component (Friston, 2005; Rao & Ballard, 1999). In support of this, studies have demonstrated a positive relationship between multisensory processing and improved accuracy, precision, and reaction times in various tasks (Alais & Burr, 2004; Ernst & Banks, 2002; Gingras et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2008). Multisensory learning has also been associated with improved detection and localization of stimuli in spatial judgement tasks (Alais & Burr, 2004; Ernst & Banks, 2002; Gingras et al., 2009).

Most research on multisensory facilitation is centered around non-verbal stimuli, but a more recent focus on verbal stimuli has emerged in the literature. Kim (2021) found that the pairing of visual and auditory presentations of the same text improved comprehension compared to when the text was learned by either reading or listening alone. In contrast, Kalyuga (2000) proposed that the learner may incur substantial cognitive load when concurrently processing multiple related sensory sources of information. Consequently, presentation of redundant information across sensory modalities may prove ineffective for learning in some cases (Kalyuga, 2000). Although congruent stimuli from multiple senses may allow for more efficient processing of information, redundant multisensory information is also useful (MacLeod, 2011; Wallace et al., 2004). When the same information is presented to multiple senses at one time (e.g., the visual presentation of a word accompanied by its auditory articulation), the presence of the information from multiple sources increases the probability that the stimuli will be recognized. Redundant multisensory information may enhance the distinctiveness of target stimuli from either sense, a process that has been thought to underlie the generation effect (Kinoshita, 1989). Therefore, the simultaneous presentation of cue and target stimuli in a typical generation task may promote its distinctiveness for later recall (Kinoshita, 1989).

Overall, the literature regarding the advantage of multisensory learning for verbal stimuli is mixed, with many asserting its benefits (Chang, 2009; Kartal & Simsek, 2017; Liu et al., 2019; Mohamed, 2018), and others finding a null (Rogowsky et al., 2016) or negative effect (Diao & Sweller, 2007; Kalyuga, 2000). For example, Diao and Sweller (2007) found that concurrent spoken presentation hindered comprehension and recall of the main ideas of a text compared to the visual-only condition (Diao & Sweller, 2007). More recent research contradicts these findings and indicates that multisensory learning improves comprehension (e.g., Kim, 2021; Liu et al., 2019; Mohamed, 2018). Additionally, students report that multisensory learning facilitates comprehension, shortens the perceived duration of tasks, enhances the appeal of learning, and improves overall sustained attention (Chang, 2009; Kartal and Simsek, 2017). Given the pervasiveness of multisensory learning in academic settings, these indeterminate results emphasize the need for further examination.

Through a similar mechanism to that proposed for the multisensory facilitation effect, the generation effect may emerge by enhancing memory for contextual information related to the generated target (e.g., the cue word; Mulligan, 2004). It has been suggested that the generation effect is more pronounced in overt tasks than in covert tasks (McCurdy et al., 2020), despite the stimuli not being congruent, which warrants further investigation.

Although the contribution of overt (i.e., auditory) verbal generation has not yet been directly examined in the generation effect literature, several studies have included spoken production alongside visual stimulus presentation in the encoding task (e.g., Gardiner & Hampton, 1985; McElroy & Slamecka, 1982; Payne et al., 1986; Slamecka & Graf, 1978). Other studies have implemented covert (i.e., silent) encoding tasks, limiting encoding to a single sensory modality (e.g., McDaniel et al., 1988; Mulligan, 2002; Mulligan et al., 2019). When visual presentation is paired with a vocalized response, the multisensory aspect of the generation task can be characterized as the provision of redundant multisensory information. Despite this, the generation effect is robust, prompting inquiry into whether the multisensory component of the task enhances its effect (increases its magnitude) compared to when an encoding task is unisensory. For instance, there is limited but intriguing meta-analytic evidence from McCurdy et al. (2020) indicating that covert generation tasks (i.e., tasks completed silently) yield slightly smaller effects as compared to overt generation tasks (i.e., tasks completed aloud).

paras.sec_title: The Role of Semantic Relatedness of Stimuli
paras.text: The semantic activation hypothesis suggests that the brain’s ability to recall information is optimized when that information is semantically related, which has been found to underlie the magnitude of the generation effect (Kinoshita, 1989; McCurdy et al., 2020). For instance, meta-analytic findings suggest that a significant generation effect emerged when words or numbers were used as stimuli, but not when nonwords were used (McCurdy et al., 2020). This finding indicates that meaningful information (e.g., words or numbers) may be a necessary condition to obtain a generation effect (McCurdy et al., 2020). The semantic activation theory of the generation effect posits that the act of generation promotes access to semantic information through a number of mechanisms. First, the act of generating a semantically related response to a given cue requires elaborative encoding of the cue word in attempt to create a connection between the new information and existing knowledge (Craik & Lockhart, 1972). The process of generation is therefore more effortful than merely reading, and this increase in cognitive effort may in part contribute to the benefit of generation in memory (Tyler et al., 1979). Non-semantic generation tasks (e.g., letter transposition) lead to smaller benefits (McCurdy et al., 2020) or nonsignificant differences (Kinoshita, 1989) in memory. Free recall is also improved by self-generation during encoding for high-meaningful words but not for low-meaningful words (Kinoshita, 1989; Nairne et al., 1985; Nairne & Widner, 1988). Taken together, these findings suggest that self-generation during encoding enhances the distinctiveness of stimuli when the cue and target stimuli are semantically related, which enhances subsequent recall of the generated information (McCurdy et al., 2020; Kinoshita, 1989).

Hypothesis 1 (H1): Based on the robust literature on the generation effect, we predicted a generation effect, as reflected by better cued recall performance for target items that were generated (e.g., Bertsch et al., 2007; McCurdy et al., 2020; Slamecka & Graf, 1978).

Hypothesis 2 (H2): We expected greater recall of target items when they are generated in the multisensory condition compared to when they are generated in the auditory or visual only condition. This hypothesis was formulated in consideration of the literature that multisensory processing improves recognition rates and accuracy of responses, and the limited but intriguing evidence that overt generation tasks yield larger effects than covert tasks (Alais & Burr, 2004; Ernst & Banks, 2002; Gingras et al., 2009; McCurdy et al., 2020).

Given that H2 specified a generation effect would emerge across all sensory conditions but would be larger in magnitude for the multisensory condition, an ordinal interaction was assessed (Elias, 2004; Park & Yi, 2024). First, the 2 × 3 factorial ANOVA specified above was conducted to assess whether sensory condition moderated the strength of the relationship between task type (read/generate) and cued recall (outcome of interest). The assumption of sphericity was not met for the main effect of sensory modality, so Greenhouse-Geisser values are reported to correct for the violation. A main effect of sensory modality did not emerge as statistically significant: F(1.77, 147.01) = 0.83, ηp2 = .01, p = .425, observed power = 0.67, and sensory modality did not significantly interact with task type: F(2, 166) = 2.03, ηp2 = .02, p = .134, observed power = 0.95. Although it was expected that a generation effect would emerge at all levels of the sensory condition, post hoc tests indicated that the generation effect only emerged for the auditory condition: Mdiff = .11, t(83) = 4.71, SE = .02, d = 0.58, p < .001, and the audiovisual condition: Mdiff = .13, t(83) = 5.41, SE = 0.02, d = 0.42, p < .001. The generation effect did not reach statistical significance in the visual condition: Mdiff = .08, t(83) = 2.95, SE = 0.03, d = 0.71, p = .062. For a visual representation of the effect across sensory conditions, see Figure 1.

We hypothesized a significant interaction between sensory modalities and task type, such that the magnitude of the generation effect was expected to increase in the multisensory condition, but the direction of the effect would not change at any level of sensory modality. To ensure the observed effects were not an artifact of the scale of measurement, a logit transformation was applied onto the dependent variable (Labaronne et al., 2023; Wagenmakers et al., 2012) and the planned analysis was repeated. The main effect of encoding survived the transformation, indicating that it was not an artifact of the original scale of measurement: F(1, 83) = 21.77, ηp2 = .21, p < .001. The main effect of sensory modality remained non-significant, F(2, 166) = 0.05, p = .950, as did the interaction term, F(2, 166) = 0.65, p = .524. A significant generation effect emerged for the auditory condition, t(83) = 3.72, SE = 0.22, p = .005, as well as for the audiovisual condition, t(83) = 4.28, SE = 0.21, p < .001. Consistent with the results obtained from the original proportions, no significant difference in cued recall performance emerged in the visual condition: t(83) = 2.28, SE = 0.26, p = .380. The size of the generation effect was not found to significantly differ as a function of sensory condition (for all comparisons, Bonferroni adjusted p = .999). In summary, the same pattern of results was observed for the logit-transformed data (see Table 4).

A third approach that was considered was soring recall as the number of correctly recalled items out of all 20 trials regardless of encoding success. However, this method may underestimate the generation effect by conflating failures of generation with failures of memory. To more directly address this limitation, an additional sample (N = 57) was tested in which feedback was provided following each generation attempt. This ensured that all participants were exposed to the intended target items, regardless of initial generation success, thereby equating encoding across conditions. Prior research indicates that an attempt to generate the correct target is sufficient to yield a generation effect, if feedback is given (Clark et al., 2021; Begg et al., 1980; Kornell et al., 2009; Potts & Shanks, 2014; Slamecka & Fevreiski, 1983). The complete pairing was displayed in all reading conditions to equate total exposure time, and feedback was given through the same modality of that sensory condition (e.g., visual feedback was shown for the visual encoding condition). Feedback was displayed for an additional 4 s after the encoding window for the target had elapsed.

Despite having a vast body of literature to rely on when examining the effect of self-generation on memory under a host of different conditions (for reviews of this literature, see Bertsch et al., 2007; McCurdy et al., 2020), the multisensory component inherent to most generation tasks has been neglected as an area of focus in this research. To help understand the mechanisms underlying the generation effect, we assessed whether the multisensory component of the task would modulate the size the effect. This examination was necessary to elucidate whether generation tasks are exemplary of the multisensory facilitation effect, or whether the generation effect is as pronounced when the multisensory component of generation tasks is absent.

In support of H1, a main generation effect was observed in the current study, which is consistent with prior literature that the benefit is robust across an array of experimental task designs (McCurdy et al., 2020). Interestingly, the significant main effect was driven by significant effects in the audiovisual and auditory encoding tasks, but no significant generation effect emerged for the visual encoding task. Although meta-analytic findings suggest that generating by speaking may yield larger effects than generation tasks that are completed by writing or typing (McCurdy et al., 2020), a plethora of studies demonstrate a significant effect for written generation tasks (for reviews, see Bertsch et al., 2007; McCurdy et al., 2020).

In consideration of transfer-appropriate processing and encoding specificity accounts (Morris et al., 1977; Thomson & Tulving, 1970), the finding of a generation effect in the auditory and audiovisual conditions, but not in the visual condition, may seem surprising. According to these accounts, memory performance is typically enhanced when the operations engaged at retrieval overlap with those engaged during encoding (McDaniel et al., 1988; Morris et al., 1977; Thomson & Tulving, 1970). The cued recall test employed in the current study required typed visual responding from the participants, regardless of the sensory modality in which the information was encoded. Therefore, one might expect the visual generation condition to benefit most from an encoding-retrieval overlap. Interestingly, however, significant generation effects emerged in the auditory and audiovisual conditions, but not in the visual condition. Although the visual generation condition arguably shared the greatest procedural overlap with the retrieval process, the current findings suggest that sensory overlap may not be a substantial predictor of performance. The central tenet of these theoretical accounts concerns the similarity of cognitive operations engaged at encoding and at retrieval, which is not constrained to mere sensory modality overlap. Therefore, it is important to consider how encoding demands may have differed qualitatively across sensory conditions to yield the observed results.

One possibility is that the auditory task facilitated phonological elaboration which enhanced the distinctiveness of the cue-target relationship, and may have also stimulated attention, compared to the silent, visual generation task (MacLeod et al., 2011). Another possibility, discussed in greater detail below, is that the visual generation task introduced greater perceptual task demands associated with typing a response under a time constraint, which may have consequently attenuated any benefit of generation. The proposed explanations are not mutually exclusive and likely interacted to influence the extent to which generation supported later retrieval across sensory conditions. Thus, the present findings do not necessarily contradict principles of transfer-appropriate processing or encoding specificity. Instead, the critical overlap in processes likely concerned cue-target relational processing required for successful cued recall performance (McDaniel et al., 1988). For the reasons outlined above, cue-target relational processing may have been encoded more distinctively in the sensory conditions that included an auditory generation component.

As proposed at Stage I of the current study, a null effect for the visual generation task may most likely indicate that the task at hand did not provide sufficient opportunity to encode the target material in the learning trials for the generation tasks. When presented with a cue word, the learner must mentally search their semantic network to generate a suitable target, given the rule and target letter provided by the researcher. This reflects the covert process of generation (i.e., thinking about the generated response). Given that overt generation mechanisms were manipulated in the current study, the covert process must then necessarily be followed by an overt generation task. The overt tasks were manipulated as (a) typing the target in the visual sensory condition; (b) saying it aloud in the auditory sensory condition, or (c) typing and then saying the target aloud in the audiovisual sensory condition. From the null effect observed only in the visual condition, where responses are only typed, we speculate that participants experienced an insufficient amount of time to overtly generate their responses. Typing out a word is more time consuming than merely saying it aloud, and perceived time pressure in the visual condition may have adversely impacted encoding in this condition. In previous studies, responses to a visual learning task were handwritten, and in the current study, responses were typed. To type a response, participants would have had to orient themselves to the layout of the keys and possibly gauge their spelling by shifting attention from the keyboard to the screen. Although typing was required for audiovisual generation as well, the typing task preceded the auditory articulation of the same generated response. Therefore, although participants may not have had sufficient time to adequately process the cue-target relationship before the next trial in the visual-only condition (Burns, 1992), the time pressure may have played less of a contributing role in an audiovisual condition.

Given the robustness of the generation effect reported in the literature across a host of experimental designs (Bertsch et al., 2007; McCurdy et al., 2020), it is unlikely that a non-significant generation effect is attributable to an absence of an actual benefit. Rather, it is more reasonable that the structure of the task itself prevented the typical generation effect from emerging. Although the time constraint in the current study was selected based on prior studies (e.g., Gardiner et al., 1988; Johns & Swanson, 1988; Kinoshita, 1989; Mulligan et al., 2019; Slamecka & Fevreiski, 1983; Slamecka & Graf, 1978), it may have been inadequate in the current sample, particularly when considering that participants had to type responses within the allotted time. To help corroborate this claim, data were collected on a separate sample where feedback was given following generation attempts. Although those analyses were not planned, the results indicated a significant generation effect in all sensory conditions. This may support the claim that in the planned methodological approach, participants experienced an insufficient opportunity to fully encode their generated response. The provision of feedback may have provided an opportunity to process and consolidate the target before attention was redirected to the next trial, thereby eliminating a perceived time pressure and improving performance. Additional work on the role of feedback would be needed to ascertain this possibility.

The rate of successful generation in the current study was relatively low, which may suggest that the present materials did not constrain responses as tightly as intended. Many other generation effect paradigms employed highly constrained cue-target relations derived, and reported higher success rates (e.g., Gardiner et al., 1988; McElroy & Slamecka, 1982; Mulligan, 2002; Mulligan et al., 2019; Slamecka & Graf, 1978). One possible explanation is that Nelson’s free association norms (Nelson et al., 2004), which were used to select the cue-target pairs, may no longer accurately reflect associative responses within the current population. Additionally, only the first letter of the anticipated target was provided, which may have been insufficient to guide participants toward a single anticipated response. Given that cue-target pairs were semantically related and participants were instructed to generate any associated word beginning with the specified letter, variability in responses is not entirely unexpected, as individuals differ in their associative networks based on prior experience (Agustín-Llach, 2023; Leger et al., 2024; Morais et al., 2013).

The total number of exposures (i.e., through auditory and visual media) was equated in the audiovisual reading condition, so a significant generation effect in the audiovisual condition is not attributable to total number of exposures to the target. The findings of the current study suggest that compared to a visual generation task, the addition of an auditory component may benefit the processing of the generated response in memory for later retrieval, particularly when the encoding window is brief. This would be consistent with the notion that the multisensory presentation of redundant information increases the probability that the stimulus will be recognized and responded to, because of its enhanced distinctiveness (MacLeod, 2011; Wallace et al., 2004). Thus, although the current results do not support the hypothesis that multisensory generation yields superior performance to unisensory generation, they do indicate that multisensory responding may, in some cases, aid processing of a cue-target relationship, particularly when the encoding interval is brief. More research is needed to ascertain this possibility.

Overall, the results do not offer uniform support for H2, which proposed that the magnitude of the generation effect would be larger for the audiovisual condition compared to either unisensory condition. The interaction between sensory modality and encoding task was non-significant, which may indicate that the effects of overt generation tasks (i.e., reading the cue word and generating the target aloud) that have been reported in the past (e.g., McCurdy et al., 2020), may be better explicated by chance error variance, or other factors. For example, multisensory generation may provide the learner with an opportunity to consolidate their covertly generated response to a greater extent than in unisensory conditions, as proposed above. Although this may yield a significant benefit under perceived time pressure, when compared to a visual task, it does not provide evidence that multisensory generation is inherently superior to unisensory generation. For example, the same benefit was not observed for the auditory comparison, suggesting that the addition of a visual component to an auditory generation task did not significantly contribute to performance. Thus, the observed pattern of results across sensory and encoding conditions might suggest that the addition of an overt articulation of a generated target is beneficial for encoding to reinforce responses under perceived time pressure, but this conclusion is speculative, given that no measure of perceived time pressure was collected. Ultimately, lack of support for H2 indicates that the multisensory component of the generation task did not uniformly improve retention of the target items compared to unisensory generation tasks.

Extant literature on the multisensory facilitation effect is mixed. Some findings suggest that multisensory processing can enhance recognition of target stimuli and improve accuracy and precision of responses (Alais & Burr, 2004; Ernst & Banks, 2002, Gingras et al., 2009). Beyond that, multisensory learning has been associated with improved comprehension outcomes (Kim, 2021; Liu et al., 2019; Mohamed, 2018), although others have found null or deleterious effects on comprehension (Diao & Sweller, 2007; Kalyuga, 2000; Rogowsky et al., 2016). In the current study, we sought to test whether the multisensory facilitation effect emerged for redundant presentations of verbal stimuli (i.e., word pairs), and further, to evaluate whether such an effect would be enhanced for generated information. First, we tested the proposal that when the same information is presented to multiple senses during learning, the probability of recognition of that stimulus is enhanced (MacLeod, 2011). Given that the effect of sensory modality was not significant, our results do not offer uniform support for this claim. Additionally, given that generating during learning is also believed to increase the probability of target recognition (McDaniel et al., 1988; Slamecka & Graf, 1978), we tested whether generated targets would be increasingly advantaged in recognition when learned under a multisensory condition, compared to passively encoded targets. Overall, our results do not offer uniform support for either claim.

The most surprising finding from the current study was a null generation effect in the visual learning condition, which is inconsistent with a large body of literature exhibiting a generation effect for written tasks (McCurdy et al., 2020). As discussed, we suggest that participants may have perceived a time pressure during the visual generation task that precluded the typical effect from being observed. To evaluate this, measures of perceived time pressure under different encoding tasks could be helpful. In the current study, exploratory analyses from a separate sample in which feedback was provided after each generation attempt offer informative evidence regarding this issue. The provision of feedback allowed encoding to be verified across sensory conditions, and under these conditions a robust generation effect emerged in the visual condition. These findings suggest that the absence of a generation effect in the visual condition may reflect a procedural constraint related to encoding demands, rather than a genuine absence of a memory benefit. Although the exploratory analysis was conducted on a smaller sample, the obtained results offer evidence that the null effect in the visual condition of the primary analysis reflected a procedural constraint rather than a true absence of an effect. In future work, it would be useful to increase the exposure time to each word pair under all conditions. Although previous studies of the generation effect have employed a 4s interval (e.g., Johns & Swanson, 1988; Slamecka & Fevreiski, 1983), a longer encoding interval may be more appropriate under the current paradigm where the participant is required to adapt to different task demands across encoding and sensory conditions. Increasing the encoding interval in future work may alleviate perceived demands and yield a typical generation effect.
